author: Jim Mosquera
title: 2019 - Disruption, Volatility And Opportunity
text:
The preceding graphic is central to my social cycle model and its influence on financial and economic market behavior in 2019. If you believe, as I do, in cyclical behavior, it's difficult to argue that we've experienced social polarization to an elevated degree. Passage through the current wintry season suggests turbulent markets ahead. What's been most telling is the polarity's extent the last few years despite many economic statistics suggesting robustness, sort of like the fight before the fight.
The genesis of this polarity might extend to the year 2000. I argued in one of my books that a very defined moment occurred in 2009 with the Tea Party demonstrations and shortly thereafter with the Occupy Wall Street event. Since that time, public discourse became, well, toxic. Perhaps not coincidentally, " toxic " was the Oxford dictionary word of the year in 2018. There's much to be gleaned about social mood from the word of the year .
I'll add little about the toxic environment in the nation's capital, though as I laid out in this text , I suspected strong contenders for the presidency in 2016 who were not cut from the traditional political cloth (Trump, Sanders). There's a full-scale political war in D.C. Wars of words and policies promote social angst and otherwise rattle markets.
Even the national pastime is showing fissures. Last season and so far this off season, the major league baseball free agent market's not moving as players and agents hoped. There's been discussion about "collusion" in the ownership ranks. ( Sorry, I know that word's been used quite a bit the last couple of years. ) Many signs point to a labor stoppage when the current agreement expires. And yes, of course it's about money, not a lack of it, but how it's distributed.
Social media's turned into a whirling pool of accusations and denunciations. Traditional news media's fed into the pool by providing less depth and more partisanship — precisely the opposite of what's needed today. The absence of a "center" can also rattle markets.
Time destroys the speculation of men, but it confirms nature.
Marcus Tullius Cicero
Financial markets and economies flourish when people feel good about their prospects. You're not going to invest in a financial instrument unless you feel good about it. You're not going to start a business venture unless you feel good about it. Sometimes the "good vibrations", to quote The Beach Boys, erupts into unabashed speculation. That speculation requires a favorable public psychology, a herding instinct and easier credit. Or as my first economic law suggests:
Credit equals confidence
Confidence will wane as the social cycle lumbers through the Winter season; credit will be less abundant. The financial speculation of the last decade will retrench. The speculative wave's defining moment crystallized for me in 2017 when I penned two articles about Bitcoin (BTC). I wrote the first one in late August 2017 and received much commentary, pro and con. The second one I penned in mid-December 2017 within a couple of days of the top in BTC. The second article offered a cautionary tale for those brave entrants into this cryptocurrency.
In March of last year, I authored an important article coming at a significant juncture in our economic and political history. The article focused on private and public debt, the stock market and interest rates. I concluded the article with the following:
All of the pieces are in place for the next recession. Consider that the political rancor of the last few years occurred with statistically strong economic data.
Investors should take steps to improve their liquidity by assuming greater cash or near-cash positions. There will be opportunities for those with liquidity. More aggressive types should look to invest in renewed volatility. Recent market action in equities is a prelude of coming attractions.
In the following lightning round, let's examine statistics showing where we've been and where we're headed.
The World
Financial Assets had their worst year in 2018 according to Deutsche Bank . China forecasts economic trouble on the horizon by promising more stimulus in 2019. Didn't excessive stimulus cause the need for more stimulus? What's the end game? Apple ( AAPL ) is keeping its fingers crossed. The IMF cut their global growth forecast in 2019. Look for the IMF to be more prominent during the next financial crisis. They may have to bail out the central bank wizards. US Business
While the retail landscape is strewn with the carcasses of Sears ( OTCPK:SHLDQ ) and Toys R Us, it's entirely another thing to have an American titan, General Electric ( GE ), have their stock price at multiyear lows; the high coming in 2000. Something common to Sears and GE was their entry into financial services. I recall reading a book by former GE chairman, Jack Welch, where he extolled the virtues of their financial arm and how profitable it was. It struck me that finance was well outside of their core business. This is yet another example of the financialization of the economy. Oh, and according to Bloomberg, GE's pension fund is $31 billion in the red. What's a zombie company? A good description might be one that has to borrow in order to pay debt. There's a pejorative term for that, beginning with the letter P and resurrecting the ghost of Madoff. Twenty percent (20%) of the Russell 2000 index and 14% of the S&P 500 are zombies . Stock Market
Despite the recent stock market selloff, traders initiated a strong round of call buying (bets on rising prices). That suggests that while psychology is fracturing, it's not anywhere near a point of capitulation. Further evidence that investors are nowhere close to crying "uncle" is reflected in the record low cash held in accounts at the brokerage, Charles Schwab. Such posture foreshadows sharp market declines. There are a number of measures reflecting overvaluation in the stock market. In this article , I discussed the market's value relative to the economy. At a minimum, expect below average returns over the next decade. For those inclined to technical analysis, both Dow Theory and Elliott Wave analysis shows a bear market in place. Credit Market
Speaking of confidence, the spread between the yield on junk debt and comparable US Treasuries narrowed to an extreme on October 3rd. What's so important about October 3rd? It happens to be the top in the stock market. What's happened to the spread since then? It's widened to a two-year high — not a sign of confidence. Indeed confidence has waned when no junk debt got issued in December. More credit = confidence news...half of the entire US investment-grade bond market is rated BBB, the lowest grade issued by S&P. The BBB market is larger now than the entire investment-grade market was in 2008. Most of this market consists of covenant-lite structures (less restrictive). These bonds are experiencing their worst year in a decade. The unwinding of this market will be chaotic when pension and other investment funds are forced to sell bonds that are no longer investment-grade. Corporate debt on steroids was great for share buybacks and dividends. The ocean of cheaply acquired debt will be more expensive to refinance. How big is this problem? Prior to the last recession, there were 54 companies rated AAA by S&P. You can now count them by making a victory sign with your index and middle finger. The leveraged loan market cratered in December. Associated leveraged loan funds witnessed historic outflows — yet another sign of diminished confidence, meaning less credit. Real Estate
While real estate is a local phenomenon, we can evaluate macro trends. As they say, your mileage may vary. Regardless of what any analyst thinks about the absolute value of home prices, affordability should remain within a constrained band. We're not within those bands. During Housing Bubble 1.0, peaking around 2005-2006, median sales prices in the US got way ahead of average hourly earnings. It took about 4 years for prices to get back in line with earnings. Housing Bubble 2.0 has created a wider divergence for a longer time. Just to get realigned with hourly earnings, median prices need to drop by 25%; again considering locality. Here's an example of extreme pricing. In San Francisco, a "starter" home is almost $900k compared to a starter household income of $35k, a ratio of 25 to 1. This doesn't mean that households with $35k income are purchasing $900k homes. It does imply that short of a winning lottery ticket, such a purchase is not contemplated, by the household or the bank. In Newark, NJ, the ratio is a tepid 8 to 1. This is still twice the traditional lending standard of 3 or 4 to 1. The US
If a work of art is worth more after it's partially destroyed , rest assured, you're at peak optimism. This really happened. A month before the October 3rd stock market top, I began using the term Omnibubble . This bubble's been dodging pins for awhile. What feeds the Omnibubble? Optimism and good will. What destroys it? Fear, uncertainty and doubt (Affordable Care Act declared unconstitutional, Paris Riots, Government Shutdown, Trade Wars). " Pay no attention to that man behind the curtain ." For all the discussion about the Fed and interest rates, it's just as instructive to watch the unwinding of their substantial balance sheet. That giant sucking sound is the money supply swirling the drain. This is quantitative easing in reverse. What the Fed gaveth, the Fed is taking away. Remember, they injected $4 trillion into the economy via their wizardry. Taking a trillion or two away will be felt. Notice that there's no mention of US government spending, funded debt, or unfunded liabilities. The wizards and our political leaders make frictionless spending decisions so forget about any fiscal probity — there's no market force presently to compel that behavior. The debts won't matter up until the point that it does and then you'll witness a new monetary order (the subject of another article).
How to approach 2019 and 2020? That depends on the type of investor . Now would be a great time to have that discussion with your financial advisor. The typical financial advisor model is predicated on a steadily rising market — investing for the long-term. Make sure you understand what long-term means. It's anathema for most advisors to stand on the sideline.
If you're a trader, this is an exciting time rife with volatility and opportunity to make bearish bets. I suspect typical investors would rather look at their statements once a month and be content with a steadily rising portfolio, especially those with retirement plans. This will be a trying time for typical investors.
At the bottom of this cycle (we're nowhere close), there will be plenty of bargains. Hopefully, you'll have the capital to avail yourself of the opportunities.
